title: Read the slow-speed coefficient
question: Why is a fast-traveler example not enough to identify the mass decrease?
recap: The low-speed coefficient identifies inertia; a finite-speed ratio is only a proxy.
premises: Newtonian kinetic energy supplies the second-order coefficient at low speed.
limitations: The quadratic approximation is not exact at finite speed.
At zero speed the ratio of the energy drop to speed squared is undefined; its limit is meaningful.

overview.text: At low speeds, energy of motion scales with speed squared. Look for that slow-speed pattern in the calculated drop. At high speeds the extra terms are too large to ignore.

full.text: For small β = v/c, γ − 1 begins with β²/2. The next term is 3β⁴/8. Keeping the second-order term gives a kinetic-energy drop of one half times L/c² times v².

full.spoken: At low speed, the kinetic-energy drop is approximately one half times L over c squared times v squared.

full.text: At the same low speed Newtonian mechanics writes the kinetic-energy drop as (m₀ − m₁)v²/2. Comparing the coefficients, rather than assuming a rest-energy formula, identifies m₀ − m₁ = L/c².

full.spoken: The limit as speed approaches zero of twice the kinetic-energy drop divided by speed squared is L over c squared.

full.returnCaption: Return to keeping the second-order term.

items: Start from the exact result: K₀ − K₁ = L(γ − 1), with γ = 1/√(1 − β²) and β = v/c.
Write γ as a power: γ is (1 − β²) raised to the power −1/2. For small x, (1 − x) to the power −1/2 equals 1 + x/2 + 3x²/8 + and so on: the binomial series, a Taylor expansion at x = 0. Put x = β².
So γ − 1 = β²/2 + 3β⁴/8 + and so on, every later term carrying a higher even power of β.
Check the series at β = 0.1: γ = 1/√0.99 = 1.0050378, so γ − 1 = 0.0050378, and the first two terms give 0.005 + 0.0000375 = 0.0050375.
At low speed keep only the first term: K₀ − K₁ is close to Lβ²/2. Replace β² by v²/c²:

steps.spoken: At low speed, the kinetic-energy drop is approximately one half times L over c squared times v squared.

items: Newton’s kinetic energy for a body of mass m at speed v is mv²/2. The speed is the same before and after, so Newton writes the drop as m₀v²/2 − m₁v²/2 = (m₀ − m₁)v²/2.
Both expressions are a coefficient times v²/2: (m₀ − m₁) in Newton’s, and L/c² in the one above. Setting the coefficients equal gives m₀ − m₁ = L/c². No rest-energy formula was assumed to get here.
The same identification, stated exactly: divide the exact drop by v²/2 and let v go to zero. From the series, 2(γ − 1)/v² = 1/c² + 3v²/(4c⁴) + and so on, so every later term vanishes in the limit:

steps.spoken: The limit as speed approaches zero of twice the kinetic-energy drop divided by speed squared is L over c squared.

items: At exactly v = 0 the quotient is 0/0 and cannot be computed; the limit is taken instead. At any nonzero speed the quotient still contains the later terms, so it is not the limiting coefficient itself.

steps.returnCaption: Return to keeping the second-order term.

margin.text: Einstein keeps only the leading term: at small speed the energy of motion is \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\), so he reads the loss of mass, \(L/V^2\), from the coefficient of \(v^2\). The higher terms matter at large speed, as the drop at 60 percent of light speed shows.
